## <span class="num">9.9.1</span> Multilinear Maps

The constructions of the previous section extend from two factors to any finite number of them.

:::definition{9.9.1} Multilinear map
Let $V_1, \ldots, V_d$ and $U$ be vector spaces over $k$. A map $m : V_1 \times \cdots \times V_d \to U$ is ***multilinear*** (or ***$d$-linear***) if it is linear in each variable when the others are held fixed. When $U = k$, $m$ is a ***multilinear form***.
:::

:::theorem{9.9.2} Tensor product of several spaces
Let $V_1, \ldots, V_d$ be finite-dimensional, and let $\mathcal{B}_i$ be a basis of $V_i$. There is a vector space $V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d$ together with a multilinear map $$\mu : V_1 \times \cdots \times V_d \to V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d, \qquad \mu(v_1, \ldots, v_d) = v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d,$$ such that for every vector space $U$ and every multilinear map $m : V_1 \times \cdots \times V_d \to U$ there is a unique linear map $\tilde{m} : V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d \to U$ with $m = \tilde{m} \circ \mu$. It is unique up to unique isomorphism, the pure tensors $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d$ with $b_i \in \mathcal{B}_i$ form a basis of it, and $\dim(V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d) = \prod_i \dim V_i$.
:::

:::proof
This is the proof of Theorem [9.8.6](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#theorem-9-8-6) with more indices. Let $V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d$ be the vector space with basis the symbols $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d$ ($b_i \in \mathcal{B}_i$). If $v_i = \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}_i} a_{i,b}\, b$, set $$\mu(v_1, \ldots, v_d) = \sum_{b_1, \ldots, b_d} a_{1,b_1} \cdots a_{d,b_d}\; b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d,$$ which is multilinear. Given $m$, the linear map with $\tilde{m}(b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d) = m(b_1, \ldots, b_d)$ satisfies $\tilde{m} \circ \mu = m$, by expanding $m(v_1, \ldots, v_d)$ using multilinearity; and it is the only linear map that can, since its values on a basis are forced. Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism is proved exactly as in Theorem [9.8.6](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#theorem-9-8-6)(iii).
:::

As before, the space can also be built as a quotient of the vector space with basis all symbols $[v_1, \ldots, v_d]$, by the relations expressing multilinearity. Linear maps $\varphi_i : V_i \to W_i$ induce a linear map $\varphi_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \varphi_d$ with $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d \mapsto \varphi_1(v_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes \varphi_d(v_d)$, since the right side is multilinear in the $v_i$; exactly as in Proposition [9.8.7](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-7), this construction is compatible with composition and identities.

:::proposition{9.9.3} Associativity
For finite-dimensional vector spaces $V_1, \ldots, V_a$ and $W_1, \ldots, W_b$, there is an isomorphism $$V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_a \otimes W_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes W_b \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_a) \otimes (W_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes W_b)$$ with $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a \otimes w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_b \mapsto (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a) \otimes (w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_b)$. In particular $(U \otimes V) \otimes W \cong U \otimes V \otimes W \cong U \otimes (V \otimes W)$.
:::

:::proof
The map $(v_1, \ldots, v_a, w_1, \ldots, w_b) \mapsto (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a) \otimes (w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_b)$ is multilinear: it is linear in $v_i$ because $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a$ is linear in $v_i$ and $\otimes$ is linear in its first argument, and similarly for each $w_j$. By Theorem [9.9.2](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#theorem-9-9-2) it induces a linear map $\Psi$ with the stated values. Choose bases of all the spaces. Then $\Psi$ sends the basis tensor $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_a \otimes c_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes c_b$ to $(b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_a) \otimes (c_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes c_b)$. The tensors $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_a$ form a basis of $V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_a$, and similarly for the $c$’s, so by Theorem [9.8.6](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#theorem-9-8-6) these images form a basis of the target. So $\Psi$ sends a basis to a basis.
:::

Thus nothing new happens with more than two factors, and we may drop parentheses in iterated tensor products.

## <span class="num">9.9.2</span> Tensor Powers and the Tensor Algebra

:::definition{9.9.4} Tensor powers
For a vector space $V$ and $d \ge 1$, the $d$th ***tensor power*** of $V$ is $$V^{\otimes d} = \underbrace{V \otimes \cdots \otimes V}_{d}.$$ By convention, $V^{\otimes 0} = k$ and $V^{\otimes 1} = V$. If $\dim V = n$, then $\dim V^{\otimes d} = n^d$. For a linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ we write $\varphi^{\otimes d} = \varphi \otimes \cdots \otimes \varphi : V^{\otimes d} \to W^{\otimes d}$.
:::

By Proposition [9.9.3](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#proposition-9-9-3), $V^{\otimes a} \otimes V^{\otimes b} \cong V^{\otimes (a+b)}$. Composing this isomorphism with the bilinear map $V^{\otimes a} \times V^{\otimes b} \to V^{\otimes a} \otimes V^{\otimes b}$ gives a bilinear multiplication $V^{\otimes a} \times V^{\otimes b} \to V^{\otimes (a+b)}$, $$(v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a) \cdot (w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_b) = v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_a \otimes w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_b,$$ which is concatenation of tensors. When $a = 0$ or $b = 0$ it is multiplication by a scalar.

:::definition{9.9.5} Tensor algebra
The ***tensor algebra*** of $V$ is the direct sum $$T(V) = \bigoplus_{d=0}^{\infty} V^{\otimes d} = k \oplus V \oplus (V \otimes V) \oplus (V \otimes V \otimes V) \oplus \cdots,$$ whose elements are finite sums $\eta_0 + \eta_1 + \cdots$ with $\eta_d \in V^{\otimes d}$, with the multiplication that extends the products $V^{\otimes a} \times V^{\otimes b} \to V^{\otimes (a+b)}$ bilinearly.
:::

:::note
$T(V)$ is a ring: the multiplication distributes over addition because it is bilinear, it has the identity $1 \in V^{\otimes 0} = k$, and it is associative because $(xy)z$ and $x(yz)$ are trilinear in $(x, y, z)$ and agree on pure tensors, where both are concatenation. It is also a vector space over $k$ whose multiplication is bilinear; a ring with this extra structure is called a ***$k$-algebra***. The tensor algebra is ***graded***: it is the direct sum of the subspaces $V^{\otimes d}$, and $V^{\otimes a} \cdot V^{\otimes b} \subseteq V^{\otimes (a+b)}$. It is not commutative once $\dim V \ge 2$: for linearly independent $u, v$, the tensors $u \otimes v$ and $v \otimes u$ are distinct elements of a basis of $V \otimes V$. As a vector space, $T(V)$ is infinite-dimensional unless $V = 0$.

The tensor algebra is the ***free $k$-algebra*** on $V$: every linear map $f : V \to A$ into a $k$-algebra $A$ extends uniquely to a $k$-linear ring homomorphism $F : T(V) \to A$ with $F(1) = 1$, namely $F(v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d) = f(v_1) \cdots f(v_d)$. This formula defines $F$ on each $V^{\otimes d}$, because the right side is multilinear in the $v_i$; $F$ is multiplicative because $F(xy)$ and $F(x)F(y)$ are bilinear in $(x, y)$ and agree on pure tensors; and $F$ is unique because $T(V)$ is spanned by $1$ and the products $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ of elements of $V$.
:::

:::proposition{9.9.6} Multilinear forms
For finite-dimensional vector spaces $V_1, \ldots, V_d$ there are isomorphisms $$V_1^* \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d^* \cong (V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d)^* \cong \{\text{multilinear forms on } V_1 \times \cdots \times V_d\},$$ under which $\ell_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \ell_d$ corresponds to the form $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto \ell_1(v_1) \cdots \ell_d(v_d)$. In particular $(V^*)^{\otimes d} \cong (V^{\otimes d})^*$ is the space of $d$-linear forms on $V$.
:::

:::proof
The second isomorphism is the universal property: $m \mapsto \tilde{m}$ is a linear bijection from multilinear forms to linear functionals on $V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d$. For the first, argue as in Proposition [9.8.13](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-13)(i): the form $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto \prod_i \ell_i(v_i)$ depends multilinearly on $(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_d)$, so it induces a linear map $V_1^* \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d^* \to (V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_d)^*$, and this map sends the tensor product of dual basis vectors $b_1^* \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d^*$ to the functional that is $1$ on $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_d$ and $0$ on the other basis tensors. So it sends a basis to the dual basis.
:::
